title: Introduction Diabetic nephropathy (DN) has become the leading cause of end-stage renal disease (ESRD) in Chinese people 1 , a phenomenon that parallels the dramatic worldwide rise in prevalence of diabetes mellitus 2 . Early detection and better management of DN patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) may delay DN progression to ESRD, lessen its complications, and improve outcome. Dysregulation of iron homeostasis is a major factor in development of DN. Increased iron stores are associated with diabetes and DN by their effect on inflammation, production of reactive oxygen species, and initiation and propagation of lipid peroxidation 3 - 5 . Conversely, iron deficiency may lead to impaired production of hemoglobin and result in iron-deficient anemia, which is common in patients with DN 6 . Disorders of iron homeostasis that occur in chronic kidney disease (CKD) turn anemia management of patients into a complex multifactorial therapeutic task 7 . New erythropoiesis-stimulating agents (ESA) such as darbepoetin 8 and others in development such as the continuous erythropoietin receptor activator 9 have longer half-lives than recombinant human erythropoietin, enabling CKD outpatients to require less frequent ESA administration. Despite the foregoing advances in CKD-associated anemia management, the one unresolved issue is the prognostic value of iron status in CKD patients. Locatelli et al. proposed serum ferritin and transferrin saturation measurements as diagnostic markers of iron status 10 . Choe et al. found that abnormal iron status increased the mortality of patients with diabetes 11 . High serum ferritin values were associated with mortality in hemodialysis patients 12 , 13 . Although the effect of iron status in clinical outcome has been examined extensively in the dialysis population 12 , 14 , there are only limited data that describe the association between iron indices and renal outcomes in the pre-dialysis population with T2DM and associated DN. Iron increases insulin resistance, and iron is related to oxidative stress in T2DM 15 . Insulin resistance and oxidative stress are risk factors for kidney progression in T2DM. Thus, it is plausible to postulate that abnormal iron homeostasis was associated with renal outcomes in patients with T2DM and associated DN. In this retrospective cohort study, we found that reduced serum transferrin was associated with diabetic ESRD. Free iron nephrotoxicity and poor nutritional status with accumulated iron or transferrin deposition might be mechanisms that contribute to DN progression. Materials and Methods Design, Setting, and Participants To investigate the association between iron status and renal outcome, this longitudinal, retrospective study included patients with T2DM and associated DN who underwent percutaneous renal biopsy from January 2010 to March 2018 at the West China Hospital of Sichuan University. All patients provided informed consent and the Institutional Review Boards of Sichuan University approved this study. The indications for renal biopsy were T2DM patients with renal damage who lacked absolute contraindications, especially T2DM patients without diabetic retinopathy, or with obvious glomerular hematuria and/or short diabetic duration, or with sudden onset overt proteinuria 16 . We used the American Diabetes Association criteria for T2DM diagnosis 17 . DN was defined based on the 2015 standard of An et al. 18 , and DN was diagnosed by at least two renal pathologists and/or nephrologists based on Renal Pathology Society (RPS) classification 19 . Adult patients with T2DM and biopsy-proven DN were eligible for this study. Exclusion criteria were coexisting nondiabetic renal diseases (NDRD) such as IgA nephropathy or systemic diseases, especially anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA) that are associated vasculitis, anti-glomerular basement membrane (GBM) disease and lupus nephritis, non-T2DM, progression to ESRD before renal biopsy, and patients who had incomplete iron status information (Figure 1 ). In sum, we enrolled 111 patients who had DN as the only glomerular disease diagnosis and for who completed iron status data were available. For tissue transferrin and iron staining, renal biopsy specimens were collected from ten potential kidney donors (healthy controls) and age, sex-matched patients with T2DN in our cohort. Table S1 displays their clinical characteristics. Clinical and pathologic information Clinical and pathologic data were abstracted from electronic medical records at the time of renal biopsy. Data included age, sex, body mass index (BMI), smoking status, presence of diabetic retinopathy, and use of renin-angiotensin aldosterone system (RAAS) blockade or ESA. Smoking status was determined at the time of biopsy. Diabetic retinopathy was defined as existence of microaneurysms, retinal dot, blot hemorrhage, or neovascularization in the retina 20 . In addition, laboratory data at the time of biopsy were obtained from the medical records. We evaluated the estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) using the creatinine-based Chronic Kidney Disease Epidemiology Collaboration equation 21 . Hematuria was defined as more than five erythrocytes per high-power field in at least two of three consecutive urine tests without urinary infection and no urinary tract malignancy or stone 22 , 23 . Treatment was defined as the use of the RAAS blockade, statins, and ESA for more than half of the follow-up period. Patient follow-up examinations were performed 2-4 times per year based on the patient's individual condition. Renal outcome was defined by the progression to ESRD, which was defined as eGFR <15 mL/min/1.73 m 2 or the need for chronic renal replacement therapy 24 . All patients were followed until March 31, 2019. Markers of serum iron status Baseline iron status at the time of renal biopsy was measured with standard protocols at West China Hospital. Serum iron concentrations and iron saturation ratios were used as indices of iron stores. Total iron-binding capacity (TIBC) was represented serum transferrin level. Transferrin was measured by chemiluminescence immunoassay, and serum ferritin was measured with an immunoradiometric assay. Serum iron and total iron-binding capacity were measured with a modified automated AAII-25 colorimetric method. Transferrin saturation (TSAT) was calculated as (iron/TIBC) *100%. Histological analysis Renal biopsy tissues for light microscopy, immunofluorescence, and electron microscopy were prepared by standard procedures at West China Hospital and examined by expert nephropathologists. Sections for light microscopy were stained with hematoxylin-eosin, periodic acid-Schiff, Masson's trichrome, and periodic acid-Schiff silver methenamine. The original biopsy results from immunofluorescence microscopy and electron microscopy were used to confirm the diagnosis of pure DN. All light microscopy pathological features evaluated in this study were based on the RPS DN classification 19 . Immunohistochemical staining Paraffin-embedded kidney tissue samples were sectioned (3 μm) and deparaffinized. Immunohistochemistry was performed as described 25 . Briefly, tissue samples were treated with 3% hydrogen peroxide in the dark to block endogenous peroxidase and then subjected to antigen retrieval by heated citric acid. The tissue samples were incubated with 3% normal goat serum (ZLI-9021, Zhongshan, China) at 37°C for 1 hour. Without washing, they were incubated with mouse monoclonal anti-transferrin antibody (sc365871, Santa Cruz, USA) at 4°C overnight and then incubated with an HRP-conjugated goat anti-mouse antibody (8125, CST, USA) at 37°C for 1 hour. Antibody binding was detected by incubating with a fresh mixture of diaminobenzidine (DAB, 8059S, CST, USA) according to the manufacturer's instructions. Slides were counterstained with Mayer's Hematoxylin, dehydrated, and mounted with Entellan (107960, Merck, Germany). Images were captured with a Nikon DXM 1200/NIS-Elements mounted on a light microscope (Nikon Eclipse E600, Shanghai, CHN) and analyzed using Image Pro Plus 6 (IPP software, Houston, TX). Staining intensity was assessed by Image Pro Plus 6 with five randomly selected images per biopsy after correction for background staining. Iron detection For iron detection, paraffin-embedded kidney tissue samples were cut into 4-μm-thick sections and deparaffinized. Then, slides were incubated in the dark with Perl's blue staining reagent according to the kit's instructions (G1422, Solarbio, China). Slides were counterstained with 0.1% nuclear fast red. Statistical analysis Continuous variables were expressed as the mean and standard deviation (SD) with symmetric distribution or as the median and interquartile ranges (IQR) with the asymmetric distribution. Categorical variables were expressed as counts and percent. Differences between continuous variables were analyzed by one-way ANOVA, followed by least significant difference (LSD) tests for multiple comparisons, or the Kruskal-Wallis H test, as appropriate. Categorical variables were analyzed using the Chi-square test or Fisher's exact test. We used Spearman's correlation analysis to assess correlations between serum iron status parameters and clinical findings. Survival cures of quartiles of serum iron, TIBC, transferrin, ferritin, and TSAT levels were obtained by Kaplan-Meier methods with a log-rank test. Univariate and multivariable Cox proportional hazard models were used to estimate the hazard ratios (HRs) for ESRD 26 . One patient was lost to follow-up and only the baseline clinical and pathologic data were analyzed for that patient. Data for 24 h proteinuria were missing for nine individuals (these nine patients were included in multivariable analyses). We first examined the differences in clinical parameters between patients with or without missing values to check whether the values were missed randomly. We then used multiple imputation methods for multivariable models. The proportional hazard assumption in Cox models was tested to check whether the dataset satisfied the basic assumptions of Cox analyses. The Cox proportional hazards model was used to calculate hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for ESRD. In the two Cox proportional hazards models, each HR was adjusted for age, sex, systolic blood pressure, eGFR, proteinuria, hemoglobin and HbA1c at the time of renal biopsy. In “Model 2”, we adjusted each HR for the aforesaid factors plus all pathological parameters as categorical variables. The clinical covariates were selected as potential confounders because of their significance in univariate analysis or on the basis of biological plausibility. Age and sex were chosen on the basis of biological plausibility, and HbA1c was selected to represent previous glycemic control. Proteinuria, eGFR, serum albumin, and hemoglobin were significant in univariate model. Parameters with P <0.05 in “Model 2” were considered significant prognosis predictors. Further, to determine the best predictors of ESRD, we used receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis with clinical/pathological variables, iron status parameters, or their combinations. The area under the curve (AUC) was calculated for each model 27 . All statistical analyses were completed using SPSS software (version 20.0, Chicago, IL, USA) and Stata SE (version 14.0, StataCorp LLC, College Station, TX, USA). Statistical tests were considered significant at P <0.05. Figures were constructed using Graph-Pad Prism 8.0 Software (Graph Pad Software, USA).

extracted_data.document_summary: This retrospective cohort study investigated the association between iron status and renal outcomes, specifically progression to End-Stage Renal Disease (ESRD), in 111 pre-dialysis patients with Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus (T2DM) and biopsy-proven Diabetic Nephropathy (DN). It found that reduced serum transferrin is an independent predictor of ESRD, and identified increased iron and transferrin deposition in renal tubular epithelial cells of DN patients, suggesting a pathological role for altered iron metabolism in disease progression.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Observational study investigating the prognostic value of iron status and related biomarkers in Diabetic Nephropathy (DN) progression.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This retrospective observational cohort study analyzed baseline serum iron status markers (serum iron, ferritin, TIBC, transferrin, TSAT) and their association with progression to End-Stage Renal Disease (ESRD) in 111 Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus (T2DM) patients with biopsy-proven DN. Serum markers were measured using chemiluminescence immunoassay, immunoradiometric assay, and colorimetric methods. Additionally, histological analysis involved immunohistochemical staining for transferrin and Perl's blue staining for iron in kidney biopsy specimens from DN patients and healthy controls. No therapeutic interventions, dose comparisons, or active treatments were investigated; the study focused on correlation and predictive value.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Lower baseline serum concentrations in ESRD patients (median 1.38 g/L, IQR 1.15-1.65) compared to non-ESRD patients; lower serum levels incrementally associated with higher ESRD risk (e.g., Q1 HR 7.36, 95% CI 1.40-38.65 vs. Q4). It positively correlated with eGFR (r=0.21, P=0.03), hemoglobin (r=0.39, P<0.001), and albumin (r=0.69, P<0.001), and negatively correlated with proteinuria (r=-0.42, P<0.001). Lower levels, especially when combined with low eGFR, predicted a worse renal outcome.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Mediates iron transport and represents total iron-binding capacity. Most important molecule for transporting iron into cells, involved in iron transport across intestinal mucosa, intracellular iron transport, and chelating free iron for non-specific immunity. Also proposed to assess nutritional status. Dysregulation of iron homeostasis is a major factor in DN development.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Progression of Diabetic Nephropathy (DN) to End-Stage Renal Disease (ESRD) in Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus (T2DM) patients; T2DM with biopsy-proven DN.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Associated with progression to ESRD, indicating poor renal outcome; a strong independent predictor of ESRD with high diagnostic value. Indicates poor nutritional status and increased susceptibility to infection; more sensitive marker of early protein depletion than albumin. Higher serum levels are associated with better renal survival.

analyzed_biomarkers.measured_tissue_or_fluid: Kidney Tissue (DN kidney biopsies, tubular epithelial cells and glomeruli)

measured_effect.direction_of_change: Higher / Absent in normal tissue, present in DN tissue
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Absent in normal kidney tissue. Positive staining observed in DN kidney biopsies, with strong positivity in tubular epithelial cells and less intense staining in glomeruli.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Iron transport and binding protein. Localized deposition can contribute to disease mechanisms. Transferrin-bound iron is potentially filtered by pathological glomerulus into the tubular lumen, leading to iron release and accumulation in tubular cells.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Diabetic Nephropathy (DN) progression, investigated in renal biopsy specimens from T2DM patients.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Suggested as a potential mechanism contributing to DN progression via tissue deposition. Indicates abnormal accumulation of transferrin and potentially iron in renal tissue, contributing to renal damage and disease progression.

analyzed_biomarkers.measured_tissue_or_fluid: Kidney Tissue (DN kidney biopsies, tubular epithelial cells)

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Deposited in a granular pattern in the tubular epithelial cells in DN, but not in controls.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Essential mineral, but free iron can cause nephrotoxicity through production of cell-damaging reactive radicals (Fenton reactions), ferroptosis (programmed cell death), and iron-induced RAS activation. Involved in iron homeostasis.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Diabetic Nephropathy (DN) progression, investigated in renal biopsy specimens from T2DM patients.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Suggested as a potential mechanism contributing to DN progression via nephrotoxicity and cell damage. Indicates a source of iron that could act on renal tubular cells, providing evidence for the role of excess tissue iron in kidney disease progression.

analyzed_biomarkers.activity_type: Protein Level / Iron Storage Marker / Concentration

measured_effect.direction_of_change: Lower (in ESRD patients), Higher (associated with diabetes/DN, potentially confounded by inflammation)
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Lower baseline concentrations in ESRD patients (median 311.0 ng/mL, IQR 168.9-555.1) compared to non-ESRD patients. Higher levels were observed in patients with lower serum transferrin quartiles. No direct relationship with renal outcomes found in this cohort, possibly due to confounding by chronic inflammation, infection, liver disease, or malignancies, which can increase ferritin concentration.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Primary intracellular iron storage protein; indicates body iron stores. Also an acute-phase reactant. Primary parameter for diagnosing absolute iron deficiency. Increased iron stores contribute to inflammation, reactive oxygen species production, and lipid peroxidation.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Development and progression of Diabetic Nephropathy (DN) in T2DM patients; associated with mortality in hemodialysis patients; T2DM with biopsy-proven DN.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicator of increased iron stores, associated with inflammation, oxidative stress, lipid peroxidation, and increased mortality risk in CKD/dialysis patients. Potential indicator for DN progression, but its utility for predicting ESRD in DN is limited due to confounding factors like inflammation, hindering accurate assessment of iron status. Lower levels are associated with ESRD, but not an independent significant predictor; high levels in patients with low transferrin may indicate altered iron metabolism.

measured_effect.direction_of_change: Lower (in ESRD patients), Higher (associated with diabetes/DN)
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Lower baseline concentrations in ESRD patients (median 10.17  5mol/L, IQR 8.00-15.70) compared to non-ESRD patients. Lower levels were observed in patients with lower serum transferrin quartiles, but not a significant predictor for ESRD in Kaplan-Meier curves.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Essential mineral; component of iron stores. Essential component of heme, involved in oxygen transport and various enzymatic reactions. Dysregulation of iron homeostasis is a major factor in DN development.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Development and progression of Diabetic Nephropathy (DN) in T2DM patients.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Index of iron stores; associated with diabetes and DN progression via inflammation and oxidative stress. Lower levels are associated with ESRD, but not an independent significant predictor; lower levels coincide with lower transferrin.

measured_effect.direction_of_change: Abnormal / Higher (in patients with lower serum transferrin quartiles)
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Median baseline was 30.9% (IQR 21.5-39.7). Higher levels were observed in patients with lower serum transferrin quartiles, but no significant relationship with renal outcomes or ESRD prediction found in this cohort due to large biological variability.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Reflects the percentage of transferrin binding sites occupied by iron; used as an index of iron stores. Indicates the percentage of transferrin binding sites occupied by iron, reflecting iron availability and transport/sequestration. Dysregulation of iron homeostasis is a major factor in DN development.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Development and progression of Diabetic Nephropathy (DN) in T2DM patients.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Diagnostic marker of iron status; associated with abnormal iron homeostasis and renal outcomes. However, not an independent significant predictor of ESRD and prone to inaccurate prediction due to biological variability; higher levels in conjunction with lower transferrin may suggest dysregulation of iron.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Higher baseline levels in ESRD patients compared to non-ESRD patients.

analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Progression to End-Stage Renal Disease (ESRD) in T2DM patients with Diabetic Nephropathy (DN).
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Higher baseline levels are associated with increased risk of progression to ESRD.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Higher baseline levels in ESRD patients (median 4.64 g/day, IQR 2.51-8.37) compared to non-ESRD patients. Negatively correlated with baseline serum transferrin (r=-0.42, P<0.001); higher levels observed in patients with lower serum transferrin quartiles.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Indicator of kidney damage and dysfunction due to protein leakage. Indicates leakage of protein from blood into urine, often due to damage to the kidney's filtration barrier.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Progression to End-Stage Renal Disease (ESRD) in T2DM patients with Diabetic Nephropathy (DN); T2DM with biopsy-proven DN.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Higher levels are associated with increased risk of ESRD, and are inversely correlated with serum transferrin, which is protective against ESRD. Marker of kidney damage; higher levels are associated with worse renal outcomes and progression of DN.

analyzed_biomarkers.activity_type: Clinical Calculation / Calculated kidney function parameter

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Lower baseline levels in ESRD patients (median 51.5 mL/min/1.73 m2, IQR 34.6-66.8) compared to non-ESRD patients. Positively correlated with baseline serum transferrin (r=0.21, P=0.03) and identified as an independent risk factor for predicting ESRD (HR 0.84, 95% CI 0.72-0.99). Low eGFR combined with low serum transferrin concentration showed high diagnostic value for predicting ESRD.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Primary measure of kidney filtering capacity. Measures kidney function, indicating the rate at which blood is filtered by the glomeruli.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Progression to End-Stage Renal Disease (ESRD) in T2DM patients with Diabetic Nephropathy (DN); T2DM with biopsy-proven DN.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Lower levels indicate worse kidney function and are associated with increased risk of ESRD; positively correlated with serum transferrin. Key indicator of kidney function; low eGFR signifies impaired kidney function and is a strong predictor of ESRD progression.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Lower baseline concentrations in ESRD patients compared to non-ESRD patients. Lower concentrations observed in patients with lower serum transferrin quartiles and positively correlated with baseline serum transferrin (r=0.39, P<0.001).

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Protein in red blood cells responsible for oxygen transport. Main protein of red blood cells, responsible for oxygen transport in the blood.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Progression to End-Stage Renal Disease (ESRD) in T2DM patients with Diabetic Nephropathy (DN); T2DM with biopsy-proven DN.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Lower levels are associated with ESRD; positively correlated with serum transferrin, suggesting a link between iron status, anemia, and kidney disease progression. Indicator of overall health and nutritional status; lower levels may suggest anemia or poor nutritional status, consistent with lower transferrin.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Lower baseline concentrations in ESRD patients compared to non-ESRD patients. Lower concentrations observed in patients with lower serum transferrin quartiles and positively correlated with baseline serum transferrin (r=0.69, P<0.001).

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Maintains osmotic pressure, transports various substances in the blood. Main protein in human blood plasma, maintains osmotic pressure, and transports various substances; a marker of nutritional status.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Progression to End-Stage Renal Disease (ESRD) in T2DM patients with Diabetic Nephropathy (DN); T2DM with biopsy-proven DN.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Lower levels are associated with ESRD, indicating poorer nutritional status or liver/kidney dysfunction; positively correlated with serum transferrin. Indicator of nutritional status; lower levels suggest poor nutritional status, consistent with lower transferrin. Transferrin has a shorter half-life, making it a more sensitive marker for early protein depletion than albumin.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Lower baseline concentrations in ESRD patients (median 35.4  5mol/L, IQR 29.32-42.2) compared to non-ESRD patients. The lowest quartile (Q1,  529.32  5mol/L) was significantly associated with increased ESRD risk (HR 3.88, 95% CI 1.14-13.25) compared to the highest quartile. Lower concentrations were observed in patients with lower serum transferrin quartiles. TIBC methods generally overestimate transferrin iron-binding capacity because iron binds to other plasma proteins.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Reflects the capacity of transferrin to bind iron, indicating iron status. Measures the total amount of iron that can be bound by proteins in the blood, primarily transferrin, reflecting the body's capacity to transport iron.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Progression to End-Stage Renal Disease (ESRD) in T2DM patients with Diabetic Nephropathy (DN); T2DM with biopsy-proven DN.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Lower levels are significantly associated with and predict an increased risk of ESRD. However, its utility for predicting ESRD in DN is limited due to overestimation and better predictive value of serum transferrin.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Lower concentrations observed in patients with lower serum transferrin quartiles.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: End product of purine metabolism; acts as an antioxidant but can also be pro-inflammatory at high levels.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Progression to End-Stage Renal Disease (ESRD) in T2DM patients with Diabetic Nephropathy (DN).
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Lower levels are associated with lower transferrin, which is linked to increased ESRD risk, suggesting a complex interplay with renal health.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Increased in a diabetic circumstance due to cytokines.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Bind transferrin to facilitate the internalization of transferrin-bound iron into cells.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Increased expression favors tissue accumulation of transferrin and deposition of iron, contributing to iron overload and potential renal damage.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Increased transferrin upregulated complement C3 synthesis.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Key component of the complement system, involved in immune response and inflammation.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: In vitro study of cultured proximal tubular cells, possibly reflecting direct effect of transferrin on renal cells in DN.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Upregulation is associated with inflammatory processes and can contribute to cell death, indicating a mechanism of renal injury by transferrin.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Potent vasoconstrictor and mediator of various physiological processes, including renal function and fibrosis.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: In vitro study of cultured proximal tubular cells, possibly reflecting direct effect of transferrin on renal cells in DN.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Upregulation is associated with vasoconstriction, inflammation, and can contribute to cell death, indicating a mechanism of renal injury by transferrin.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Increased transferrin upregulated monocyte chemoattractant peptide-1 expression.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Chemokine that regulates the migration and infiltration of monocytes/macrophages, key players in inflammation and tissue injury.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: In vitro study of cultured proximal tubular cells, possibly reflecting direct effect of transferrin on renal cells in DN.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Upregulation is associated with recruitment of inflammatory cells and can contribute to cell death, indicating a mechanism of renal injury by transferrin.
